content:
Panel 5: Optimising Networks: From networks of expertise (NoEs) and clusters into future ways of working and collaborating
Networks of Expertise (NoEs) generate valuable evidence, tools, and collaborations in palliative care, but translating these outputs into enduring change remains a challenge. This panel will explore how network findings can move beyond publications to shape routine practice, policy, training, and ongoing professional collaboration. Panellists will discuss what elements should be sustained after NoEs conclude, and how professional organisations such as the EAPC can lead efforts to standardise approaches, support scale-up, and embed network outputs into everyday palliative care practice across Europe.
Panellists: Stein Kaasa ( JANE2), Cinzia Brunelli (EUonQOL and QOL Cluster), Carlos Centeno (EAPC Atlas), Erna Michiels (Hope4Kids), Phil Larkin (CODE-YAA)

properties.Session: TS: Innovative methods for implementation of digital tools in palliative care: insights from the 4D-PICTURE project
properties.Chairs: None Guillaume Economos, Dr Zuzana Křemenová

content:
Research into the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital tools in Palliative Care.

Increasingly, digital tools are developed to enhance the quality, accessibility, and coordination of care for persons with serious, life-limiting illnesses. While some tools are promising, few (less than 15%!) are sustainably adopted in practice. Key reasons are that such tools: a) lack a system approach, b) lack decent stakeholder collaboration; and c) are insufficiently integrated in complex, diverse care paths.   In the seven-country EU/UKRI funded 4D PICTURE project (2022-2027), we design, evaluate and implement digital decision-support tools in oncology and palliative care, and develop innovative methods to improve their implementation (https://4dpicture.eu/). This transdisciplinary project spans palliative care, public health, design, implementation science and many more disciplines. In this theme session, we demonstrate our ongoing work, and use prognostic tools and communication tools as case studies. We provide recommendations for the applicability of the three methods in diverse European palliative care settings. 
Introduction: Judith Rietjens, professor Design for Public Health.

Aims and learning objectives:To demonstrate three promising methods to improve the implementation of digital tools in palliative care:

1.	The digital NASSS implementation framework, to analyse the complexity of digital tools in seven domains and provide solution pathways to improve them;

2.	The Remote Participatory Bodystorming method, to gather stakeholder feedback on digital tools throughout their developmental process;

3.	The service design method MetroMapping, to visualise and redesign care paths to allow seamless integration of digital tools. 

After the session, participants have a clear understanding of the three methods. They leave with hands-on inspiration on how to use them across diverse palliative care settings.

content:
Panel 6: Engaging with policy
This panel will explore how research consortia can strategically engage policymakers at EU, national and regional levels through timely evidence synthesis, policy briefs, stakeholder alliances, and alignment with legislative and funding cycles. The session will highlight practical approaches to ensure palliative care evidence informs sustainable policy development across Europe.
Panellists: Nancy Preston (Pal-Cycles, EU PAL-COPD and PalSed), Tadeusz Hawrot (PsyPal), Tania Pastrana (RAPHAEL)
Panel 7: The Future of EU Funding Calls: 
This panel will examine the new EU health research funding landscape, including mission-oriented approaches, public–private partnerships, widening participation mechanisms, and increasing emphasis on digital transformation, resilience, and implementation impact. The session will explore how the palliative care community can strategically position itself within future EU agendas to secure sustainable investment and strengthen its contribution to European health policy and systems innovation.
Panellists: Andreja  (RAPHAEL), Cinzia Brunelli   (EUonQOL), Dirk Hadrich   (EU Cancer Mission)

properties.Session: EAPC Groups: Global Caregiving in Focus: An Interactive Session to Guide Research, Health Systems, and Policy
properties.Chairs: Prof Clare Gardiner, Dr Aline De Vleminck, Dr Viktoria Wallin

content:
Designed to foster dialogue and collaboration, this interactive session hosted by the EAPC Reference Group for Family Caregiving aims to advance and prioritise the international research and policy agenda for family caregiving. Prof Gardiner will provide an overview of emerging concepts in family caregiver research and present updates from the EAPC White Paper for Family Caregiving. Interactive ranking tools will be used to solicit audience input on emerging research priorities. Prof Hudson will outline progress on the proposed Lancet Commission on family caregiving, which will provide global strategies to improve the well-being of family carers. Interactive tools will be used to collate audience views on policy solutions and effective interventions to contribute to the Commission.  Prof De Vleminck will provide an update on emerging interventions and technology innovations supporting family caregiving. A global perspective will provide a ‘state of the science’ and a novel perspective on harnessing technology to support carers.

The aims and learning objectives:
The aim of this interactive session is to provide an overview of new and emerging innovations in family caregiving and engage delegates in identifying priorities for advancing this field of research. The learning objectives are to: 
1. Educate attendees on new and emerging concepts and innovations in family caregiving, including global policy, technology innovations and research approaches. 
2. Facilitate audience engagement to actively co-produce ranked research priorities and capture stakeholder views to inform health policy and practice. 

Speakers: 
Prof Clare Gardiner, Professor of Palliative Care, UK 
Prof Peter Hudson, Director Centre for Palliative Care c/o St Vincent’s Hospital and The University of Melbourne ,Australia 
Prof Aline De Vleminck, Associate Professor at the End-of-life Care Research Group, Free University of Brussels (VUB) and Ghent University, Belgium

All speakers are members of the EAPC Reference Group for Family Carers.

TS: Researching new horizons for integrated, community-oriented health systems
properties.Chairs: Prof Scott Murray, Dr Libby Sallnow

content:
Research into Primary Care.

This dynamic and participatory session builds on recent global discussions and research around community-oriented primary palliative care, highlighting as care shifts to community settings, integration of palliative care within primary care is more essential.  The first presentation will share new international data on compassionate community interventions and outcomes. The second will explore implementation and evaluation of interventions in primary palliative care, focusing on equity, continuity, and measurable outcomes. The final speaker will present an emerging conceptual definition of primary palliative care as a bridge across systems, communities, and care providers. An interactive segment will follow, inviting delegates to co-create components of a shared definition using tools such as digital boards and word clouds. This collaborative process aims to advance a more inclusive and globally resonant framework for primary palliative care, aligned with WHO’s vision for universal health coverage. The session brings together researchers and practitioners from across continents and disciplines.

Aims and learning objectives:

This session explores innovative pathways to integrate palliative care within primary health systems, emphasising community-oriented care, measurable outcomes, and global equity. Participants will:

•	Examine global data and indicators essential for evaluating compassionate community models.

•	Reflect how palliative care can best be recognised, valued, and measured in primary care 

•	Understand a broader conceptualisation of primary palliative care

•	Engage in proposing a new research and policy agenda that integrates community capacity, informal networks, and lay caregiving into mainstream palliative care strategies and indicators
